hints: Notice the dashed cell box contains e.m.f. $E$ in series with internal resistance $r$, so the total circuit resistance is $R + r$.
Recall $I = E/(R + r)$ and terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$, where $Ir$ is the voltage lost inside the cell.
Check what happens to $Ir$ when $R$ is made smaller and $I$ changes, then decide if $E - Ir$ gets larger or smaller.
walkthrough: Identify the single-loop circuit: e.m.f. $E$ drives current $I$ through internal resistance $r$ and external variable resistor $R$ in series.
Use $I = E/(R + r)$ with constant $E$ and $r$. Decreasing $R$ decreases the denominator $R + r$, so $I$ increases.
Use terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$. The term $Ir$ is the lost volts across the internal resistance.
Since $I$ is larger and $r$ is constant, $Ir$ is larger, so $V = E - Ir$ is smaller. Current increases and terminal p.d. decreases. This is option C.

options.A: Current does not decrease because total resistance $R + r$ decreases, so $I$ must increase.
options.B: Current increases rather than decreases, and terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$ falls when $I$ rises.
options.C: Total resistance falls so $I = E/(R+r)$ increases, and larger lost volts $Ir$ leaves smaller terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$.
options.D: Current does increase, but terminal p.d. cannot increase because more voltage is lost across the internal resistance.
